Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For a civilian assault trauma, 'talks about military' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the assault specifically involved military context, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It is not supported by the other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' implies a trauma involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty context. That does not cohere with the rest of this profile, which otherwise describes an individual assault without any indication that others were killed.

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: This appraisal is the main incoherent item in the profile. The rest of the report is organized around fear, betrayal, hypervigilance, male-related/interpersonal triggers, and fragmented sensory trauma memory after assault. In contrast, fearing that she will lose control of her own rage and do something terrible introduces a perpetration/anger-control theme that is not supported by the triggers, threat items, or memory content. It does not fit the dominant cognitive formulation in which negative appraisals feed threat and memory; the other appraisal items plausibly amplify fear and mistrust, but this one points to a different clinical concern not otherwise represented in the profile. Given the otherwise tightly fear-based assault presentation, this item is hard to integrate clinically with the selected set.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: This threat item is the least coherent element in the profile. The rest of the selected triggers, appraisals, and memory items consistently describe an interpersonal assault formulation centered on men, betrayal, mistrust, conversational/emotional triggers, and trauma memories. By contrast, needing to stay alert at night implies a more generalized ongoing danger-monitoring pattern that is not specifically supported by the selected triggers or appraisals. It is not impossible in PTSD, but here it fits less well than the other threat items and is weakly linked to the formulation, especially because Threat has no active edge to Maladaptive Strategies and the profile lacks other nighttime/sleep-related material.

vignette: Elena had been thirty-eight when the man she shared a home with turned their kitchen into a space of sudden violence. It began during a discussion about their future, the kind of conversation they had circled for years, until a familiar phrase about boundaries struck a raw nerve. Before she could step back, he lunged. The memory would never settle into a coherent story for her. When she tried to explain the night to her husband later, or to the officers who arrived, her tongue grew heavy. She could only manage flashes: the sharp angle of his elbow, the smell of burnt garlic lingering from the stove, the weight of his hand pinning her wrists to the counter. Her body remembered what her mind refused to sequence. Years later, when a clinician asked her to recount the event, Elena’s shoulders would hike to her ears, her hips would tilt exactly as they had when she was trapped, and she would stare at the wall until the room stopped spinning. She had come to believe that the night could not be spoken, only endured in the sudden, silent architecture of her posture. The months that followed dissolved into a state of constant readiness. Elena found herself scanning every room she entered, her eyes catching on shadows near doorways, her pulse spiking whenever a door handle turned without warning. Strangers approaching her on the sidewalk, even when they were simply asking for directions or holding out a flyer, sent her nerves into immediate defense; she would cross the street or press herself against a brick wall until their footsteps faded. The open kitchen of her restaurant became a space of acute sensory friction. When a line cook dropped a tray or reached swiftly across the pass to grab a knife, Elena’s body reacted as if the threat were real again. She flinched so violently once that a sous chef spilled a pot of stock, and she spent the rest of the shift gripping the edge of the prep table, her breath coming in short, controlled pulls. She was certain that danger could arrive without warning, that the person standing closest was often the one who would strike, and that her only option was to remain permanently watchful. Over the next several years, Elena’s avoidance calcified into quiet routine. She stopped discussing anything that felt remotely familiar to that evening, steering conversations toward weather, menu logistics, or the stock market whenever a certain cadence of voice or a particular word drifted too close. Emotional closeness became a source of quiet dread. When her husband tried to hold her longer or speak softly about his fears, she would gently but firmly step back, convinced that intimacy was merely a precursor to unpredictability. She told herself that people could not be trusted, that loyalty was easily overturned, and that she had been foolish to lower her guard. In her restaurant, the avoidance took a different shape. She stopped assigning prep shifts to the male line cooks, opting instead to manage the station herself or request female staff whenever possible. She avoided the walk-in cooler after midnight, and when male suppliers came to inspect deliveries, she kept the service door propped open and stood near the registers. Her husband noticed the distance, the way she flinched when he reached for her hand, the quiet exhaustion that settled over their weekends. She did not argue; she simply rationalized the distance as necessary insulation. Now at fifty-four, Elena walks into the intake room with her shoulders squared and her gaze fixed on the middle distance. The PCL5 score of 68 reflects the sheer volume of days she spends braced for impact. She came to therapy because the kitchen, once her sanctuary, now feels like a stage set for collapse, and because her marriage has grown quiet in a way that frightens her as much as the past. She does not expect to relive the night in full, nor does she think it will ever make logical sense. What she hopes for is simply to stop her body from answering to ghosts, to sit across from a man without calculating his exit route, and to believe, even for a moment, that closeness does not inevitably lead to harm. She still wonders who will hurt her next, but for the first time, she is asking someone to help her figure out how to stay present when the answer remains unknown.
